strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: converting naturally occurring conversational feedback into preference-training data. The 20,281-pair dataset and model-specific variants constitute a potentially useful resource, and the pipeline is clearly motivated.

Experiments cover three model families, two data-generation strategies, and three established benchmarks. Substantial improvements over the starting models support practical utility beyond the proposed evaluator: Phi-3's AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate increases from 24.3% to 34.9%, and Arena-Hard performance from 15.4% to 32.4%.

The paper reports conversation- and user-disjoint evaluation, human validation of feedback detection and checklist evaluation, detailed annotation rubrics, model identifiers, and core training hyperparameters. DSAT precision of 83.3% supports the feasibility of mining useful feedback. Selection bias and unsafe preferences are explicitly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved alignment with actual users is insufficiently validated. GPT-4 extracts preferences, generates preferred responses, filters on-policy pairs, and evaluates responses using those extracted preferences. Increased checklist scores therefore establish adherence to inferred preferences more directly than faithful recovery of users' preferences. The 200-conversation human study reports 57.14% agreement versus 63.27% human-human agreement, but evaluates checklist application rather than independently validating preference extraction or demonstrating improved user alignment in the trained models.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of conversational feedback. WildFeedback and regenerated UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversational context, and response-selection procedures. A control using the same WildChat prompts and comparable generation budgets without feedback, or with generic refinement instructions, is needed to distinguish feedback-specific benefits from domain matching and distillation. No SFT-only comparison establishes the additional benefit of the constructed preference pairs.

Reproducibility remains incomplete for a contribution centered on a dataset and custom benchmark. The dataset is described as 'available soon,' without an accompanying artifact link. The FAISS-based test construction omits the embedding model and sufficient similarity and deduplication details; the hyperparameter search does not specify its validation and selection protocol. These gaps materially limit reconstruction despite the useful prompts and final training settings.

The claims of consistent and significant superiority over UltraFeedback exceed the reported results. For Qwen-2 with GPT-4-generated data, WildFeedback scores below UltraFeedback on AlpacaEval LC (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66). Several other advantages are small, and no confidence intervals or training-seed variability are reported.

The evaluation supports a narrower population than the claims about diverse, evolving user needs and majority preferences suggest. Feedback-bearing conversations are selective, DSAT recall is only 48.4%, and the custom test deliberately selects central preferences within clusters and tasks resembling training data. The acknowledged selection bias is therefore consequential to interpreting the results. Together with the missing controls and incomplete reproducibility, this leaves the paper borderline for Findings despite credible benchmark gains.
